journal_name: ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a fundamentally new theoretical framework for dynamic criticality adaptation in mixed-criticality embedded systems, challenging the conventional assumption of static criticality levels during runtime. Traditional mixed-criticality scheduling theory relies on pre-defined criticality modes that cannot flexibly respond to workload variations in modern cyber-physical systems. We propose the Probabilistic Criticality Continuum (PCC) model, which treats criticality as a continuous, context-dependent parameter rather than discrete levels. The PCC framework introduces novel schedulability analysis based on stochastic demand-bound functions that capture the full spectrum of timing requirements. We derive sufficient and necessary conditions for feasibility under the PCC model and prove that our approach dominates existing mode-switch based methods in terms of resource utilization. The theoretical contribution includes polynomial-time algorithms for computing criticality thresholds and adaptive scheduling parameters. Furthermore, we establish connections between PCC and classical real-time scheduling theory, demonstrating that our paradigm provides a unifying framework that subsumes existing approaches as special cases. Evaluation on synthetic workloads and automotive case studies reveals up to 47% improvement in system flexibility while maintaining hard real-time guarantees for critical tasks.

This paper presents improved response time analysis for multiprocessor real-time scheduling using partitioned fixed-priority algorithms. While existing analysis techniques provide sufficient but overly pessimistic schedulability tests, our work achieves significantly tighter bounds through a novel busy-window propagation model. We first identify critical inadequacies in current worst-case interference calculations for multi-core embedded systems, particularly the overestimation of context-switch overheads and cache-related preemption delays. Our improved analysis introduces the concept of interference locality windows, which accurately captures how task migrations affect execution patterns in system-on-chip architectures. We derive new sufficient schedulability tests with pseudopolynomial complexity and further propose an efficient polynomial-time approximation with bounded worst-case performance loss of 12%. Compared to state-of-the-art analysis methods, our approach achieves schedulability ratio improvements of 18-31% across various task set configurations. The theoretical results are validated through extensive simulation studies using synthetic workloads conforming to realistic embedded system characteristics. Additionally, we provide exact response time formulas for specific priority assignment policies commonly used in automotive and avionics embedded applications.

This paper presents EMBAYES, a novel Bayesian-inspired hardware/software co-design framework that fundamentally transforms how cyber-physical systems adapt to uncertain operating environments. Traditional co-design methodologies employ deterministic models that fail to capture the inherent uncertainty in sensor networks and physical system dynamics. EMBAYES introduces probabilistic design space exploration using Bayesian optimization integrated with hardware synthesis, enabling automatic discovery of energy-quality tradeoffs at design time while maintaining rigorous worst-case guarantees. The framework comprises three key innovations: (1) a hierarchical uncertainty modeling architecture that separates epistemic and aleatory uncertainty sources, (2) a multi-fidelity design exploration engine that efficiently navigates the joint hardware-software parameter space, and (3) a runtime adaptation layer that leverages offline design insights for online decision-making. We implement EMBAYES as an open-source framework supporting FPGA-based system-on-chip generation and demonstrate its effectiveness through three case studies: an autonomous navigation controller, an industrial process monitoring system, and a wireless sensor node. Results show that EMBAYES achieves 3.2x faster design convergence compared to conventional multi-objective evolutionary approaches while producing implementations with 28% lower energy consumption under equivalent quality constraints.

This paper presents RealFlex, a comprehensive fault-tolerant embedded operating system architecture that significantly advances reliability mechanisms for mixed-criticality automotive applications. RealFlex addresses critical limitations in existing embedded operating systems by introducing a hierarchical isolation framework combining hardware-enforced spatial isolation with software-managed temporal isolation, specifically optimized for modern multi-core system-on-chip platforms with hardware virtualization support. The system architecture implements three key mechanisms: (1) a lightweight hypervisor layer providing deterministic interrupt handling and memory protection with overhead under 5% compared to bare-metal execution, (2) an adaptive fault detection module using hardware performance counters for early detection of timing anomalies and transient faults, achieving 94% fault coverage with false positive rates below 0.1%, and (3) a novel checkpoint consolidation algorithm that minimizes rollback costs for mixed-criticality applications with diverse real-time requirements. We prototype RealFlex on an ARM Cortex-A53 platform running realistic automotive workloads and demonstrate graceful degradation under injected fault scenarios. Experimental results show 2.4x improvement in fault detection latency compared to software-only approaches, while maintaining hard real-time guarantees for safety-critical functions with jitter below 50μs. The system supports legacy application integration through POSIX-compatible interfaces.
